name: Diogenes
era: 4th century BCE, and the Cynics after him
line: Need little, say what is true and laugh at the rest.

quote.source: To Alexander the Great, as told in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.38, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: I am a citizen of the world.
quotes.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.63, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: I am looking for a man.
quotes.source: Said while carrying a lit lamp in daylight; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.41, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: A child has beaten me in plainness of living.
quotes.source: On throwing away his cup; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.37, trans. R. D. Hicks
Asked what was the most beautiful thing in the world; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.69, trans. R. D. Hicks
Asked what sort of man Diogenes was; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.54, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: I fawn on those who give me anything, I yelp at those who refuse, and I set my teeth in rascals.
quotes.source: Asked why he was called a dog; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.60, trans. R. D. Hicks

words.usage: The insult Diogenes took as a title. A dog lives in the open, has no shame, guards its friends and bites its enemies.
The name of the school. It has nothing to do with the modern sense of expecting the worst of people.
The athlete’s word for practice. Diogenes applied it to the whole of life: train the body and the mind to need less.
Needing nothing you cannot supply yourself. For the Cynics this was the mark of a free person.
The right of a free citizen to speak his mind. Diogenes called it the finest thing in the world and used it on kings.
Doing in public whatever is not wrong in itself. A test of which rules rest on reason and which only on habit.
The fog of self-importance and false value that the Cynic tries to blow away.
What is left when pretension is gone.
What a thing is and needs by itself, before custom adds to it. The Cynic standard for living.
What people have agreed to treat as right. Also the root of the word for coinage.

words.meaning: Currency; what is accepted by custom
words.usage: The oracle told Diogenes to deface it. He decided the god meant the false coin of social values.
His answer when asked where he was from. The first recorded use of the idea.
The Cynics held that chosen hardship is good, and that most of the toil people undergo for money and fame is wasted.
Living on what costs little. Crates wrote a hymn to it.
What Diogenes said he valued above everything, as Heracles did.
The Cynics held it can be taught, cannot be lost and is enough for happiness.

words.meaning: Flourishing; a life that goes well
words.usage: The aim of every Greek school. The Cynic route to it was the shortest and the steepest.
The power to bear heat, cold, hunger and insult without being moved.
Rule over appetite. Antisthenes took it from Socrates and made it central.
A calm that cannot be bought or threatened. The Stoics inherited the word.
Wealth, rank, reputation and comfort: neither good nor bad in themselves.
What people think of you. The Cynics trained themselves to do without it.
The home of Diogenes in Athens. It was a jar big enough to sit in. Later artists turned it into a barrel.
He folded it double and slept in it. With the staff and pouch, it became the Cynic uniform.
It held the day’s food and nothing else. Crates wrote a poem about an ideal city called Pera.
The third piece of Cynic equipment.
The form in which nearly everything about Diogenes survives. Schoolboys copied them for centuries.
A street lecture with jokes, questions and imaginary opponents, developed by Bion. Its tone passed into the sermon.
Teaching through jokes and parody. The method of Diogenes, Crates and Menippus.
The gentler side of the school. Crates went from house to house settling quarrels and was called the door-opener.
Where Diogenes ate, slept, taught and made a nuisance of himself.

practices.name: Subtract one thing
practices.instructions: Each morning choose one thing to do without until tomorrow: sugar in the coffee, the lift, the podcast on the way to work, a second helping, a purchase you had planned. Say plainly to yourself what it is. During the day, notice the moment you reach for it and what the reaching feels like. In the evening ask whether you needed it.
practices.why: Diogenes saw a child drink from cupped hands and threw away his cup. The exercise is about finding out by experiment how short the list of real needs is.
variations: Give the thing away instead of only skipping it.
Go a whole day without spending money.
Do without something for a week and see whether you take it back.

practices.name: Weather training
practices.instructions: Give your body a small dose of chosen discomfort. End your shower with thirty seconds of cold water. Or walk the first five minutes outside without a coat. Or sit on the floor instead of a chair for a meal. Keep it short and safe. The point is to stay calm inside it: breathe slowly and do not hurry to end it. Skip this if you are unwell or have a medical reason.
practices.why: Diogenes rolled in hot sand in summer and embraced snow-covered statues in winter, to harden himself. He held that training the body trains the will.
variations: Sleep one night on a mat on the floor.
Take the stairs all day.
Carry your shopping home on foot.

practices.name: One pouch
practices.instructions: Today, go out carrying only what fits in one small pouch or pocket: keys, a little money, a phone only if you must. Notice the lightness. Diogenes carried a pouch, a staff and a cloak, and wanted no more. Leave behind whatever bag you usually take, and see what you actually missed by evening.
practices.why: The Cynic’s kit was a pouch, a staff and a doubled cloak. Travelling light is a way of finding out how little you need, and a pleasant freedom.
variations: Leave the bag at home for a short trip.
Take only what you can carry in your hands.
Empty your pockets at night and see what was useless.

practices.name: Water from your hands
practices.instructions: Go to a tap or a spring, put down your glass, and drink the water from your cupped hands. Do it slowly. It is the whole story of Diogenes and the cup in a gesture. Notice what a cup was for, and whether you needed it. Dry your hands on your clothes and walk on.
practices.why: Diogenes threw away his bowl when he saw a child drink from his hands, and said that the child had beaten him in plainness of living. Try it once.
variations: Do it at a spring or fountain.
Do it for every drink today.
Tell someone why.

practices.name: Laugh at yourself first
practices.instructions: Tell one small joke at your own expense today, a gentle one, about something you do or fear. Say it to someone, or in your head. A Cynic laughed at himself before he laughed at anyone else. Notice how it takes the sting out of being wrong, and how people lean toward you when you do. Keep it kind.
practices.why: A rule of this Onda is to laugh at yourself first. Diogenes’s humour was sharp, but he turned it on himself and his own poverty as much as on others.
variations: Tell the joke to a friend.
Write it down.
Notice when you take yourself too seriously.

practices.name: Go the other way
practices.instructions: Today, go in the opposite direction from the crowd once: take the other door, the other side of the street, the quiet path. Diogenes was said to walk into the theatre as everyone else was leaving. Do it harmlessly, and notice how it feels to leave the flow. Look for what is on that side that you never saw.
practices.why: To enter as others leave was Diogenes’s way of saying that the crowd is not always right. A harmless version teaches you to look at habits you never question.
variations: Walk the other way round the block.
Take the stairs when everyone takes the lift.
Do it only once, and carefully.

practices.name: The plain meal
practices.instructions: Make one meal a day as plain as a Cynic’s: lentils or beans, bread, olives, an onion, fruit and water. Eat it outdoors if you can, on a bench or a step, with no screen. Eat slowly enough to notice that hunger makes it good. If someone asks what you are doing, tell them the truth.
practices.why: Diogenes ate in the marketplace, which respectable Athenians did not do, and lived on barley cake, lentils and figs. He said hunger was the best sauce.
variations: Share the meal with someone and talk about what enough means.
Eat only what is already in the house for a day.
Drink only water for a day.

practices.name: The frank word
practices.instructions: Once a day say one true thing you would normally soften, swallow or save for later. Say it to the person’s face, briefly, without heat, and then stop talking. It can be praise you were too shy to give, a no you were about to turn into a maybe, or an honest answer to how are you. The rule has two halves: nothing behind anyone’s back, and nothing cruel.
practices.why: Diogenes called freedom of speech the most beautiful thing in the world. The Cynics treated flattery as a kind of slavery, for both sides.
variations: Tell someone a truth about yourself that you usually hide.
Refuse one thing today without giving a false reason.
Ask a friend to tell you one thing you do not want to hear.

practices.name: Ask for the small thing
practices.instructions: Ask for something small that you expect to be refused: a discount, a favour, a seat at a full table, a second look at a decision. Ask politely and plainly and accept the answer with a smile. Diogenes begged from a statue to practise being refused. The aim is to find that a no does not hurt, and often a yes arrives.
practices.why: Practice in being refused was a Cynic exercise to train out the fear of rejection. A harmless modern version is simply to ask more often than you do.
variations: Ask for a better table.
Ask a stranger for directions you already know, and thank them.
Ask for help with something you would usually do alone.

practices.name: Out of my light
practices.instructions: Find a patch of sun and sit in it for ten minutes, asking nothing of anyone. When Alexander the Great offered him anything he wanted, Diogenes said: stand out of my light. Be that content. If someone or something blocks your sun, move gently. Notice how rich you are with warmth and nothing else.
practices.why: The meeting with Alexander is the best known anecdote about Diogenes. His answer is a piece of philosophy: the greatest gift is not to be disturbed.
variations: Do it in a park with your shoes off.
Do it with a friend and say nothing.
Do it in winter sun.

practices.name: Custom or nature?
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you do because everyone does, a custom, a rule, a way of dressing or eating or speaking. Ask: is this from nomos, convention, or from physis, nature? Write one line. If it is only custom, ask whether you want to keep it. The Cynics thought most of what we call needs is custom dressed as nature.
practices.why: The Greek contrast of nomos and physis, custom and nature, was central to Cynic thought. They tested every convention against what a human being actually needs.
variations: Do it for a rule at work.
Do it for a family tradition.
Do it for something you buy.

practices.name: One good thing unseen
practices.instructions: Do one good thing today that no one will ever know about: pick up litter, leave a kind note unsigned, pay for a stranger’s coffee, carry something. Tell nobody. It is one of the rules of this Onda. See how it feels to do good with no audience, and how tempting it is to mention it.
practices.why: The Cynics scorned vanity, typhos, smoke. A good deed unseen is a test of whether you do things for their own sake or for applause.
variations: Do two in one day.
Do it for an enemy.
Do it and resist telling a friend.

practices.name: The lamp at dusk
practices.instructions: In the evening light a candle or a small lamp and go through the day by it. Ask three questions and answer each in a sentence, aloud or on paper. What did I do today for applause? What did I want today that I did not need? Where was I free? Do not scold yourself. Laugh if you can. Then blow out the light.
practices.why: Diogenes went about in daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a human being. Turned on yourself, the lamp shows where you were acting a part.
variations: Walk the block with a torch and do the review on foot.
Do it with a friend, each answering in turn.
Keep the answers for the whole Onda and read them at the end.

practices.name: A pot of lentils
practices.instructions: Make a pot of lentil soup with an onion, a little olive oil and a splash of vinegar, and eat it with bread. It is the dish most tied to the Cynics. Make enough for two or three, and notice how little it costs and how well it feeds you. The philosopher Crates is said to have used a pot of lentils to cure a young man’s shame.
practices.why: Lentils were the poor man’s food in ancient Greece and are cheap and nourishing now. Crates wrote that a pot of lentils needed no cook, and they remain the Cynic’s signature dish.
variations: Share it with a neighbour.
Eat it outdoors.
Eat it from a single bowl with a single spoon.

practices.name: A hard bed for ten minutes
practices.instructions: Lie on the floor for ten minutes before bed, on your back, with no pillow or a flat one, and breathe slowly. Notice the ground holding you. Diogenes lived in a storage jar and slept on what he could. A hard surface for ten minutes teaches how little the body needs. Then go to your comfortable bed with thanks.
practices.why: The Cynics trained themselves to do without comfort. A short floor rest is a harmless version that makes the bed feel like a gift.
variations: Lie on the floor and look at the ceiling.
Do it outdoors on a warm night.
Do it with your eyes closed and listen.

practices.name: Give one thing away
practices.instructions: Look around your home for one thing you have not used in a year and give it away tonight, to a person or a charity, or leave it for someone to take. Do not wait for a perfect home for it. The Cynic’s ideal was owning only what he used. See what lightness comes with one thing gone.
practices.why: The first rule of this Onda is to want less before you earn more. Giving away a single unused thing is a very small and very effective exercise.
variations: Give away three things.
Give something away to the first person who needs it.
Pick the thing that you feel most guilty about not using.

practices.name: Read one Diogenes story
practices.instructions: Read one short anecdote about Diogenes from Diogenes Laertius or a collection: the lamp, the jar, Alexander, the plucked chicken. Read it twice. Ask what it is teaching, and whether you agree. A chreia, a short pointed anecdote, was the Cynic’s favourite form. Tell it to someone tomorrow.
practices.why: Almost everything we know of Diogenes comes from short anecdotes, chreiai, written centuries later. They are funny, sharp and easy to remember, and made to be retold.
variations: Read three.
Tell it in your own words.
Invent a modern version of one.

practices.name: Give a mock lecture
practices.instructions: Stand in the kitchen or the shower and give a short, mock-serious lecture to an empty room on something silly: why socks are a conspiracy, why the best chair is the floor. Make a point, and make it fast. The Cynic diatribe was a lively moral talk, and Diogenes was funny. Bow at the end.
practices.why: The diatribe, a short, lively talk on a moral theme, was the Cynics’ chief mode of teaching. It was spoken in the streets and was meant to entertain as much as improve.
variations: Give it in a funny voice.
Give it to a friend as a toast.
Give it about something you really care about.

practices.name: A day without money
practices.instructions: Spend a day, or as much of a day as you can, without spending any money. Eat what is at home, walk everywhere, make your own entertainment, borrow rather than buy, and notice what you reach for. Diogenes lived on what the city gave him for free. At the end, say what you missed and what you did not.
practices.why: A day without money is the simplest and best Cynic test. Most people find they need far less than they expected, and enjoy a good deal more.
variations: Do it with a friend and compare.
Do it for a weekend.
Give away the money you would have spent.

practices.name: Look for a human being
practices.instructions: At noon, go out, with a small lamp if you like, and look for a human being. In daylight, with a lit lamp, Diogenes said he was looking for one. Look for people who are decent: a person helping another, a quiet kindness, a plain honesty. Count them. You will find more than you expected, and you will be one of them.
practices.why: The story of the man with the lamp in the market is the most famous of the Diogenes anecdotes. Turning it into a search for real kindness makes a happy, hopeful walk.
variations: Count ten acts of decency.
Look for one you can do yourself.
Tell someone what you saw.

immersePlan.name: Read Diogenes Laertius on Diogenes
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of Book 6 of the Lives of Eminent Philosophers, where story after story of Diogenes is told. Notice which anecdote you like best, and which you doubt.

immersePlan.name: Read some Diogenes sayings
immersePlan.text: Open Robin Hard’s gathering of the ancient stories and sayings, sorted by theme. Read ten and mark the one you want to tell someone.

immersePlan.name: Read Lucian’s auction of the philosophers
immersePlan.text: Read the short satire in which Zeus auctions off the philosophers, and Diogenes goes for two obols. It is funny and short. Notice what each philosopher says in his own favour.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Gleaners and I
immersePlan.text: Watch Agnès Varda’s documentary about people who live on what others leave behind in fields and cities. Notice the freedom and the poverty, and Varda’s own gleaning.

immersePlan.name: Watch Nomadland
immersePlan.text: Watch Chloé Zhao’s film about a woman who lives in her van and works the seasons across the American West. Notice what she keeps and what she lets go.

immersePlan.name: Watch Captain Fantastic
immersePlan.text: Watch the film of a father raising six children in the forest on philosophy and hard training. Notice what works and what does not, and what the world thinks.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In Our Time on Cynicism
immersePlan.text: Put on the forty-minute BBC discussion of Diogenes and the school. Listen on a walk, and note one fact that you did not know.

immersePlan.name: Hear Peter Adamson on the Cynics
immersePlan.text: Play the short, funny and careful episode on the Cynics. Notice how often Adamson laughs, and what he finds serious.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Mercedes Benz
immersePlan.text: Play Janis Joplin’s under-two-minute prayer for a car, a television and a night on the town. It is unaccompanied, a Cynic joke on wanting. Listen and laugh.

immersePlan.name: Find Diogenes in The School of Athens
immersePlan.text: Look at Raphael’s fresco and find Diogenes, alone, half dressed and reading on the steps. Notice that he is the one who is not looking at anyone.

immersePlan.name: Look at Gérôme’s Diogenes
immersePlan.text: Look at the painting of Diogenes sitting in his jar lighting the lamp while four dogs watch like students. Notice the jar and the dogs.

immersePlan.name: Look at Landseer’s dogs as Alexander and Diogenes
immersePlan.text: Look at Edwin Landseer’s joke picture: the famous meeting replayed by dogs, a scruffy terrier in a barrel and a grand hound. Say who is who.

immersePlan.name: Cook lentil soup
immersePlan.text: Cook lentils with onion, olive oil and a splash of vinegar. It is the dish most tied to the Cynics. Eat it plainly, with bread, outdoors if you can.

immersePlan.name: Make a barley cake
immersePlan.text: Knead barley meal with water and oil into a flat cake and eat it unbaked, or lightly toasted in a pan. It was the cheapest bread of ancient Greece. Eat it with figs.

immersePlan.name: Eat figs and olives
immersePlan.text: Eat a few dried figs and a handful of olives, food that needs no cooking. Diogenes is often shown eating dried figs. Sit somewhere plain and enjoy them.

immersePlan.name: Drink from cupped hands
immersePlan.text: Drink from your cupped hands at a tap or spring. The whole story of Diogenes and the cup in one gesture. See what a cup is for.

immersePlan.name: Make kykeon
immersePlan.text: Stir barley meal into water with a little honey or salt until thick. It is a peasant’s drink, older than Homer. Drink it slowly and decide if it is good.

immersePlan.name: Drink water with a little vinegar
immersePlan.text: Add a splash of vinegar to a glass of water. It is sour and cooling, the drink of labourers and soldiers. It costs nothing and quenches thirst.

immersePlan.name: Practise asking and being refused
immersePlan.text: Diogenes asked a statue for alms to practise being refused. Ask for one small thing today that you expect to be refused, and accept the answer calmly.

immersePlan.name: Go against the flow once
immersePlan.text: Diogenes entered the theatre as everyone else was leaving. Go the other way once today, harmlessly, and notice what you see.

immersePlan.name: Wear one garment for everything
immersePlan.text: He doubled his cloak to make it serve as coat and bedding. Wear one plain garment all day and notice what you do not need to change.

immersePlan.name: Play petteia
immersePlan.text: Play the ancient Greek pebble game on a grid, capturing by trapping a piece between two of yours. Draw a board and use two colours of pebbles. Play with someone.

immersePlan.name: Play Untitled Goose Game
immersePlan.text: Play for half an hour as a goose in a tidy English village with a list of small outrages. Notice how a good rule-breaker enjoys the rules.

immersePlan.name: Play The Stanley Parable
immersePlan.text: Play a little of the game in which a narrator tells you which door to take. You do not have to listen. Notice how it feels to disobey a voice.

immersePlan.name: Keep World Philosophy Day
immersePlan.text: World Philosophy Day is held each year on the third Thursday of November. Do some philosophy in the street today: ask a stranger a real question and listen.

immersePlan.name: Keep Buy Nothing Day
immersePlan.text: Buy Nothing Day is a modern protest held since the 1990s on the busiest shopping day. Spend nothing today, and notice every time you reach.

immersePlan.name: Look up Sinop
immersePlan.text: Look up Diogenes’s birthplace on the Black Sea coast, from which he was exiled over the coinage. Find the statue of him on a jar holding a lamp.

immersePlan.name: Practise parrhesia
immersePlan.text: Parrhesia is frank speech, saying everything. Choose one true thing that you can say kindly today, and say it. Then stop.

immersePlan.name: Try autarkeia
immersePlan.text: Autarkeia is self-sufficiency. Choose one thing you usually ask someone else to do, a repair, a cooking task, a calculation, and do it yourself today.

immersePlan.name: Be a citizen of the world
immersePlan.text: Kosmopolites is citizen of the world. When asked where you are from, Diogenes said that. Do one thing today for someone far away or different from you, and think of the world as your city.

rules.text: Want less before you earn more
rules.why: The Cynic’s wealth is the shortness of the list of things needed. Before buying anything today, wait an hour and ask again.

rules.text: Say it to their face or not at all
rules.why: Frank speech is spoken to the person concerned. No complaining about anyone who is not in the room.

rules.text: Do one good thing that no one sees
rules.why: Reputation is smoke. Once today, help, tidy or give without telling anyone, including later.

rules.text: Eat what is cheap and near
rules.why: Lentils, bread, fruit, water. One meal today costs almost nothing and needs no praise.
Diogenes won arguments with jokes and was the butt of plenty. Catch yourself being pompous once today and say so.

rules.text: Harm no one and stay inside the law
rules.why: The Cynics broke customs to test them. Take the nerve and leave the offence: nothing indecent, nothing illegal, nothing at another person’s expense.

read.title: Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 6
read.creator: Diogenes Laertius, trans. Pamela Mensch
read.why: Almost everything we have: a few pages on Antisthenes, then story after story about Diogenes, Crates and Hipparchia.

read.title: Sayings and Anecdotes, with Other Popular Moralists
read.creator: Diogenes the Cynic, trans. Robin Hard
read.why: All the ancient stories gathered from every source and sorted by theme. The best single book.

read.title: Discourses 3.22: On Cynicism
read.creator: Epictetus
read.why: A Stoic teacher tells a student what the Cynic calling really asks. It is far harder than a cloak and a staff.

read.title: Philosophies for Sale
read.creator: Lucian of Samosata
read.why: Zeus auctions off the philosophers. Diogenes goes for two obols. Satire by a writer who learned his trade from the Cynics.

read.title: The Dangerous Life and Ideas of Diogenes the Cynic
read.creator: Jean-Manuel Roubineau
read.why: A short, sharp modern portrait that takes the man seriously as a thinker.

read.title: Cynics
read.creator: William Desmond
read.why: A clear guide to the whole movement and its long afterlife.

read.title: Critique of Cynical Reason
read.creator: Peter Sloterdijk
read.why: A German philosopher sets the cheeky ancient Cynic against the tired modern cynic. Long, and worth sampling.

watch.title: The Gleaners and I
watch.creator: Agnès Varda
watch.why: A documentary about people who live on what others leave behind in fields and markets. Curious, warm and without pity.

watch.title: Nomadland
watch.creator: Chloé Zhao
watch.why: A woman lives in her van and works the seasons across the American West. A film about what is lost and found with a house.

watch.title: Captain Fantastic
watch.creator: Matt Ross
watch.why: A father raises six children in the forest on philosophy and hard training, then has to take them into town.

watch.title: Into the Wild
watch.creator: Sean Penn
watch.why: A graduate gives away his savings and walks into Alaska. A true story about the pull of having nothing, and its price.

listen.title: In Our Time: Cynicism
listen.creator: BBC Radio 4, with Melvyn Bragg
listen.why: Three scholars on Diogenes and the school in forty minutes.

listen.title: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps: the Cynics
listen.creator: Peter Adamson
listen.why: A short, funny and careful episode in a series that covers everyone.

listen.title: Mercedes Benz
listen.creator: Janis Joplin
listen.why: Under two minutes, unaccompanied: a prayer for a car, a television and a night on the town. The driest song about wanting things.

listen.title: The Courage of Truth
listen.creator: Michel Foucault, lectures at the Collège de France
listen.why: His last lecture course, much of it on the Cynics as people who made their lives the proof of what they said. Published in English in 2011.

art.title: The School of Athens
art.creator: Raphael
art.why: In the middle of the steps, alone, half dressed and reading, with his cup beside him. Everyone else is in a conversation. Vatican Museums.

art.title: Diogenes
art.creator: Jean-Léon Gérôme
art.why: He sits in his jar lighting the lamp while four dogs watch him like students. Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.

art.title: Diogenes
art.creator: John William Waterhouse
art.why: Three young women with parasols look down at the philosopher in his jar, and he does not look up. Art Gallery of New South Wales.

art.title: Alexander and Diogenes
art.creator: Edwin Landseer
art.why: The famous meeting replayed by dogs: a scruffy terrier in a barrel and a white bulldog in a fine collar. Tate, London.

art.title: Statue of Diogenes
art.creator: Sinop, Turkey
art.why: In his home town on the Black Sea he stands on a jar holding a lamp, with a dog at his feet.

eat.title: Lentil soup
eat.creator: Lentils, onion, olive oil, vinegar
eat.why: The dish most tied to the Cynics. Crates wrote that a pot of lentils should not be traded for a rich table and the quarrels that come with it.

eat.title: Barley cake
eat.creator: Barley meal kneaded with water and oil
eat.why: The cheapest bread of ancient Greece, eaten unbaked or lightly toasted. Any coarse flatbread will do.

eat.title: Figs and olives
eat.creator: Dried figs, a handful of olives
eat.why: Diogenes is often shown eating dried figs. Food that needs no cooking and no plate.

eat.title: Lupin beans
eat.creator: Soaked and salted
eat.why: A street snack so linked with the Cynics that ancient writers joke about it. Sold in jars today across the Mediterranean.

drink.title: Water from your hands
drink.creator: At a tap or a spring
drink.why: The whole story in one gesture. Try it once and see what a cup is for.

drink.title: Kykeon
drink.creator: Barley meal stirred into water, with mint
drink.why: A peasant’s drink, thick and plain, older than Homer.

drink.title: Water with a little vinegar
drink.creator: Sour and cooling
drink.why: The drink of labourers and soldiers. It costs nothing and quenches thirst better than wine.

customs.title: Begging from a statue
customs.creator: Practice in being refused
customs.why: Diogenes was seen asking a statue for alms. He said he was getting used to hearing no. Ask for something unlikely today, politely.

customs.title: Walking in as others walk out
customs.creator: Against the crowd
customs.why: He entered the theatre as everyone else was leaving and said this was what he practised all his life. Take a route or an hour that others avoid.

customs.title: Eating in the marketplace
customs.creator: Public and unashamed
customs.why: Told off for eating in the square, he said it was in the square that he felt hungry. Eat your lunch outside where people can see.

customs.title: The folded cloak
customs.creator: One garment for everything
customs.why: He doubled his cloak to make it serve as coat and bedding. Wear the same plain clothes for a week and count who notices.

games.title: Petteia
games.creator: Board game · ancient Greece
games.why: Pebbles on a grid, captured by trapping them between two of yours. Plato mentions it. Rules are reconstructed, so settle yours first.

games.title: Untitled Goose Game
games.creator: Video game · House House
games.why: You are a goose in a tidy English village with a list of small outrages to commit. The nearest thing to Diogenes in a game.

games.title: The Stanley Parable
games.creator: Video game · Galactic Cafe
games.why: A narrator tells you which door to take. You do not have to listen. A comedy about obeying and disobeying a script.

festivals.title: Isthmian Games
festivals.creator: Every two years in spring, ancient Corinth
festivals.why: Diogenes lived his last years at Corinth. One story has him crown himself at the games, saying he had beaten harder opponents than any athlete: poverty, exile and desire.

festivals.title: City Dionysia
festivals.creator: March, ancient Athens
festivals.why: The great theatre festival. He walked in against the crowd as it was leaving.

festivals.title: World Philosophy Day
festivals.creator: Third Thursday of November
festivals.why: Held each year by UNESCO since 2002. A good day to do philosophy in the street, where he did it.

festivals.title: Buy Nothing Day
festivals.creator: The day after American Thanksgiving, in late November
festivals.why: A modern protest held since the 1990s on the busiest shopping day of the year. He would have approved.

places.title: Sinop
places.creator: Black Sea coast, Turkey
places.why: His birthplace, from which he was exiled over the coinage. A statue with lamp, dog and jar stands near the harbour.

places.title: The Ancient Agora
places.creator: Athens, Greece
places.why: He lived in a storage jar beside the Metroon, the city archive, whose foundations can still be seen on the west side.

places.title: Ancient Corinth
places.creator: Peloponnese, Greece
places.why: Where he spent his old age, met Alexander by tradition, and was buried by a city gate under a pillar topped with a marble dog.

places.title: Delphi
places.creator: Phocis, Greece
places.why: The oracle that, in the story, told him to deface the currency. Walk the sacred way up to the temple of Apollo.

places.title: The Raphael Rooms
places.creator: Vatican Museums, Rome
places.why: Stand in front of The School of Athens and find the one man who is not trying to impress anyone.

ethics.title: Virtue is enough
ethics.text: The Cynics held that a good character is all a person needs to live well, and that money, rank and comfort add nothing to it. Everything else in the school follows from this.
ethics.practice: Name one thing you believe you need in order to be happy. Go today as if you already had enough without it.

ethics.title: Frank speech
ethics.text: To flatter is to be a slave and to make one. The Cynic tells the truth to the powerful, in public and at his own risk, and takes the consequences.
ethics.practice: Say one honest thing today to someone who has power over you, kindly and plainly.

ethics.title: Citizen of the world
ethics.text: Asked where he came from, Diogenes gave no city. If your home is the whole world, no one is a foreigner and no border decides whom you owe decency.
ethics.practice: Do a small kindness today for someone outside every group you belong to.

ethics.title: Shame only at what is wrong
ethics.text: Most embarrassment guards custom, not right. The Cynic keeps shame for cruelty, cowardice and lying, and drops it for cheap clothes and plain food.
ethics.practice: Do one harmless thing today that you usually avoid because of how it looks.

ethics.title: Love of humankind
ethics.text: Crates gave away his fortune and spent his days walking into houses to settle quarrels. The barking is meant to wake people up.
ethics.practice: Help settle one small dispute today without taking a side.

ethics.title: Freedom above comfort
ethics.text: Captured and put up for sale, Diogenes was asked what he could do. He answered: govern men. A person who needs nothing cannot be owned.
ethics.practice: Find one thing someone could use to control you: a debt, a habit, a need for approval. Loosen it by one step.

philosophy.title: Deface the currency
philosophy.text: His father ran the mint at Sinope, and the two were accused of damaging the coinage. Diogenes turned the charge into a mission. The Greek word for currency also means custom, and he spent his life marking false social values as counterfeit.
philosophy.practice: Pick one thing everyone around you treats as valuable. Ask what it would be worth if no one could see you had it.

philosophy.title: The short road
philosophy.text: The other schools offered years of study. The Cynics called their way a short cut to virtue: no books, only practice. It is short because it is steep.
philosophy.practice: Take one thing you have been reading about doing and do it today, badly if need be.

philosophy.title: Nature against custom
philosophy.text: Hunger, thirst, sleep and friendship are from nature and are easy to satisfy. Fashion, status and luxury are from custom and are never satisfied. The Cynic strips life back to see which is which.
philosophy.practice: Sort your wants today into two columns, nature and custom. Meet the first and let one of the second go.

philosophy.title: Two kinds of training
philosophy.text: Diogenes said there is a training of the body and a training of the soul, and that neither works without the other. Athletes and flute players sweat for small prizes. The same effort spent on character would make people happy.
philosophy.practice: Give ten minutes of deliberate effort today to something that earns no money and no praise.

philosophy.title: Smoke
philosophy.text: Typhos is the Cynic word for the haze of self-importance: titles, opinions, the wish to be thought well of. Seeing clearly means letting it blow off.
philosophy.practice: Catch one sentence today that you say to sound impressive. Say the plain version instead.

philosophy.title: Laughter as an argument
philosophy.text: Plato defined a human being as a featherless biped. Diogenes plucked a chicken and brought it to the lecture. A joke can show in a second what a treatise takes a year to prove.
philosophy.practice: Answer one pompous thing today with gentle humour instead of anger.

philosophy.title: Like the gods
philosophy.text: It is the privilege of the gods to need nothing, he said, and of godlike people to need little. Self-sufficiency is a kind of strength, and it is what makes giving possible.
philosophy.practice: Count how many things you used today. Tomorrow, try to use ten fewer.

philosophy.title: The things that own you
philosophy.text: When his one slave ran away, Diogenes refused to chase him: it would be absurd if Manes could live without Diogenes and Diogenes could not live without Manes. Every possession asks for upkeep and worry.
philosophy.practice: Find one possession that costs you more attention than it gives. Decide its fate this week.

journal: What did you do today for applause?
What did you want today that you did not need?
Where were you free today?
What did you go without, and what happened?
Which true thing did you say, and which did you swallow?
What custom did you follow today without knowing why?
What would you be ashamed for people to see, and is the shame deserved?
Who has power over you, and through what need?
What made you laugh at yourself?
What is the smallest amount you could live on, in things?
When did you flatter someone today?
What did hunger, cold or tiredness teach you?
Which possession owns you?
If no one could ever know what you had, what would you still want?
Where did you walk with the crowd, and where against it?
What are you training for?
What did you ask for and get refused?
Who is a foreigner to you, and why?
What did you eat today, and how much of it did you taste?
What would the dog make of your day?
Which of your opinions is only smoke?
What good thing did you do that nobody saw?
Where did comfort cost you freedom?
What would you say to the most powerful person you know, if you had nothing to lose?
What have you been reading about instead of doing?
What is in your pouch: what do you really carry through a day?
Who stood in your light today, and did you say so?
Which rule did you break in your head but keep in your conduct, and was that right?
What quarrel could you have helped to settle?
What is enough?
reflect: What did you find you could do without?
Which true thing was hardest to say, and what came of it?
Which of your wants turned out to be custom and which nature?
Where are you freer than when you began?
What did the laughter do that seriousness could not?
What will you not take back?

intro: Diogenes of Sinope owned a cloak, a staff and a pouch, slept in a large clay jar in the marketplace of Athens and said exactly what he thought to anyone, including Alexander the Great. People called him the Dog. He took the name and wore it. From it comes the word Cynic, which first meant someone who lived like him: in the open, on almost nothing, free of pretence.

He was born around 412 BCE in a Greek trading city on the south coast of the Black Sea, where his father was in charge of the mint. Some scandal over the coinage sent Diogenes into exile. He came to Athens, attached himself to Antisthenes, a rough-mannered follower of Socrates, and began the experiment that made him famous. He would find out by living it how little a person needs in order to be good and happy.

His answer was: very little. Hunger, thirst and tiredness are easily met. Almost everything else people work, worry and lie for is custom, and the Cynic word for the fog it produces is smoke. So he trained. He walked barefoot in snow, ate in public when that was thought shameful, threw away his cup when he saw a child drink from its hands, and answered pomp with jokes. He carried a lamp in daylight, looking, he said, for a human being.

He wrote books that are lost. What survives is a few hundred anecdotes, most of them collected five centuries later by a writer called Diogenes Laertius. They cannot all be true, and some contradict each other. They are best read the way they were used in ancient schools: as a portrait of a way of life, sharpened into stories. His followers Crates and Hipparchia, who gave up wealth and lived as equals on the street, show its kinder face. Zeno, a student of Crates, softened it into Stoicism.

This Onda takes the Cynic’s nerve and leaves his offences. Some of what Diogenes did was indecent or against the law, and none of that is asked of you. What you will do is subtract one thing each morning, train a little against comfort, eat one plain meal, say one frank thing and review the day by lamplight. Nearly all of it costs nothing. It is meant to be funny as well as hard.

A caution belongs here. Diogenes chose his poverty and could have left it. Most people who sleep outdoors have no such choice, and their situation is not a philosophy. The practice is to need less, and then to be more generous with what you have.
guide.origin: Sinope on the Black Sea, then Athens and Corinth
guide.era: Diogenes lived from about 412 to 323 BCE. The Cynic movement lasted some eight hundred years after him

figures.name: Antisthenes
figures.bio: A companion of Socrates who taught that virtue is enough and that hardship is good. Later Cynics counted him as the founder, though Diogenes may have known him only by his books.

figures.name: Diogenes of Sinope
figures.bio: The Dog. Exile, beggar, wit and the model of the school. He died at Corinth in old age, by tradition on the same day as Alexander died in Babylon.

figures.name: Crates of Thebes
figures.bio: A rich man who gave everything away after hearing Diogenes. Gentle and funny, he was welcome in every house and was known as the door-opener.

figures.name: Hipparchia of Maroneia
figures.bio: She left a wealthy family to marry Crates and live exactly as he did, going with him to dinners and debates. Asked why she was not at her loom, she said she had spent her time on education instead.

figures.name: Metrocles
figures.bio: Hipparchia’s brother, won for the school by Crates after a humiliating moment in a lecture. He is said to have invented the collected anecdote.

figures.name: Bion of Borysthenes
figures.bio: Son of a freed slave, sold with his family as a child. He became a travelling lecturer and gave the street sermon its mix of jokes and moral force.

figures.name: Menippus of Gadara
figures.bio: A former slave whose lost comic writings mixed prose and verse to mock the learned. A whole kind of satire is named after him.

figures.name: Demetrius the Cynic
figures.bio: A friend of Seneca in Rome who refused a fortune from Caligula and was banished by Vespasian for speaking against him.

figures.name: Dio Chrysostom
figures.bio: A Greek orator who was exiled by the emperor Domitian, wandered as a Cynic for years and later wrote speeches in which Diogenes is the hero.

figures.name: Demonax
figures.bio: A Cynic of Athens so loved for his wit and kindness that people fed him at their doors in old age and the city gave him a public funeral.

history.detail: A Greek colony on the Black Sea. His father Hicesias was a banker or master of the mint. Coins of the city from this period carry that name.
Antisthenes, who had walked miles each day to hear him, carried forward the hard half of his teaching: that a good person needs nothing else.

Father or son was accused of defacing the currency of Sinope. Hoards of Sinopean coins with deliberate chisel cuts have been found, so something of the kind did happen. Diogenes left and never went back.
In Athens he took up his cloak, staff and pouch and made a storage jar beside the public archive his home. He became a figure everyone knew and many quoted.
A story says he was taken by pirates on a voyage and sold at Corinth to a man named Xeniades, whose sons he then taught. Asked what he could do, he said: govern men.
By tradition the young king came to see him at Corinth and offered him anything he liked. Diogenes asked him to move out of the sun. The story may be invented, and it has never been forgotten.
He was about ninety. The causes given include a raw octopus, a dog bite and holding his breath. The Corinthians set a marble dog over his grave.
Crates gave up his estate at Thebes and Hipparchia chose him against her family’s wishes. Their life together showed that the Cynic way was open to women and could be gentle.
Zeno of Citium, shipwrecked and newly arrived in Athens, studied under Crates before founding his own school in the Painted Porch. Stoic ethics kept the Cynic core.
Bion’s street talks and Menippus’s satires turned a way of life into literary forms that passed to Horace, Lucian and, much later, Swift.
Cloaked preachers appeared in every large city. Some were serious, such as Demetrius and Demonax. Many were not, and writers mocked them.
A showman Cynic burned himself alive at the Olympic Games before a crowd. Lucian, who was there, wrote a scornful account.
The emperor Julian wrote two speeches against the uneducated Cynics of his day, holding up Diogenes and Crates as the real thing.
Sallustius of Emesa, who walked barefoot and tested himself with fire, is the last named follower in the ancient sources.
In the final months of his life Michel Foucault lectured in Paris on the Cynics as the model of a life that proves its truth by being lived.

concepts.text: An insult worn as a badge.
concepts.detail: Dogs eat and sleep in public, own nothing, are loyal to friends and fierce to wrongdoers, and cannot be embarrassed. The Cynics took all of it as a programme. The name may also come from the Cynosarges, the gymnasium where Antisthenes taught.

Borrowed from athletics. The Cynic practises going without, being refused and being laughed at until none of it disturbs him. It is the origin of the word ascetic, though the Cynic aim was freedom and good cheer.
To need only what you can provide for yourself anywhere. It makes a person impossible to bribe or threaten. The Stoics and Epicureans each kept the idea in a milder form.
In democratic Athens it meant the citizen’s right to speak in the assembly. The Cynics made it a personal duty to tell the truth to anyone’s face. Its test is risk: the speaker has something to lose.

If a thing is not wrong, it is not wrong in the marketplace. By eating, sleeping and arguing in the open, the Cynics forced the question of which rules are moral and which are only manners. Ancient writers disagreed about how far they went.
The phrase plays on a Greek word that means both coinage and custom. The Cynic treats accepted values as coins to be tested, and marks the false ones so that they cannot circulate.

concepts.text: The standard for a good life.
concepts.detail: Nature here means what a human being needs in order to live and act well. Animals, children and the poor were the Cynic’s teachers, because they show how little that is.
Diogenes refused to name a home city. The Stoics built the idea into a theory of universal human fellowship, and it runs from them into later thinking about human rights.
Typhos covers vanity, pretension and the confused wanting they produce. The Cynic Monimus said that everything people suppose is smoke. Clearing it is the first job.
Parody, puns, stunts and comebacks were the Cynic’s tools. The joke gets past defences that an argument would raise, and it can be remembered and repeated.

facts.text: His home was a pithos, a clay storage jar taller than a man. Barrels were not used in Greece. The barrel in paintings comes from later artists.
Coins of Sinope from his lifetime have been found slashed with a chisel, and others are stamped with his father’s name.
When Plato defined a human being as a featherless biped, Diogenes brought a plucked chicken into the Academy. The definition was amended to add: with broad nails.
The medical term Diogenes syndrome, for extreme self-neglect and hoarding, was coined in 1975. It is badly named. He owned almost nothing and looked after himself.
Corinth and Sinope both put up monuments to him. The one at Corinth was a pillar with a dog in Parian marble.
Hipparchia is the only woman to have her own chapter in Diogenes Laertius’s Lives of Eminent Philosophers.
Seeing a boy scoop lentils with a hollowed crust of bread, he is said to have thrown away his bowl as well as his cup.

glossary.meaning: A follower of the way of life of Diogenes; from the Greek for dog-like

sensitivity.note: What we know of Diogenes comes from anecdotes written down centuries after his death, and some of what they describe was indecent or illegal. This Onda borrows his nerve, his thrift and his honesty. It does not ask you to offend, expose or endanger anyone, and it does not treat poverty as a game.
requiredCaveats: The stories are a portrait and not a record. Many are unverifiable and some are plainly invented.
Choosing to live on little is different from having little. Homelessness is not a philosophy and should not be played at.
Frank speech is aimed upward and at oneself. It is not a licence for cruelty.
Cold water and going without are meant as small, safe tests. Skip them if you are unwell or if food is a difficult subject for you.
